title: DIP: Dependency Inversion Principle
description: High-level policy should not depend on low-level detail: abstractions, injection, ownership of the interface and the composition root.

questions.text: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle say?

options.text: Interfaces must live in separate assemblies
High-level modules should depend on abstractions, and so should low-level modules, rather than policy depending on concrete details
Always use a dependency injection framework

questions.explanation: Business policy should not import a specific database or mail library. Both sides depend on an abstraction that the high-level code defines and owns.

questions.text: `OrderService` does `new SqlOrderRepository()` in its constructor. What is the main cost?

options.text: It cannot be tested without a database and cannot switch storage without editing the service

questions.explanation: Creating the concrete class inside ties policy to a detail. Taking an `OrderRepository` abstraction in the constructor lets tests pass a fake and production pass the SQL version.

questions.text: Which statement distinguishes dependency inversion from dependency injection?

options.text: Injection is a principle, inversion is a framework
Inversion is the design rule about the direction of dependencies; injection is one technique to supply the implementation

questions.explanation: Inversion decides who depends on whom (details depend on policy's abstractions). Injection (constructor, setter, container) is a way to hand the chosen implementation in.

questions.text: In a layered design, who should own the `PaymentGateway` interface?

options.text: The business layer that needs payments, with the adapter implementing it

questions.explanation: Inversion means the abstraction is shaped by the needs of the high-level module. Then the adapter depends on the business layer, not the reverse.

questions.text: Where should concrete classes normally be chosen and wired together?

options.text: In the composition root, near the application entry point

questions.explanation: One place that knows all the concrete types keeps the rest of the code free of them. That place is the composition root (a `main`, a startup file, a container configuration).

questions.text: Using an interface for every single class, even one that will never have a second implementation, is required by DIP.
questions.explanation: False. DIP matters at the boundaries where detail changes or needs faking (databases, clocks, network). Wrapping stable internal helpers in interfaces adds noise.

questions.text: Which of these are signs of a DIP violation?

options.text: A domain class imports an ORM or HTTP client namespace
Business code calls `DateTime.Now` directly and tests need sleeps
A service creates its own collaborators with `new`

questions.explanation: Domain code that names infrastructure types, hidden clocks and self-created collaborators all weld policy to detail. Constructor injection of an abstraction is the remedy.

questions.text: A test needs to prove a retry runs after the third failure, without waiting for real time. Which design helps most?

options.text: Inject an abstraction of time/delay so the test can control it

questions.explanation: Time is a dependency like any other. Injecting a clock or scheduler lets tests advance it instantly.
